extracted.intended_audience: medical journal editors, authors submitting to medical journals, and journal publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for preparing, submitting, and publishing scholarly articles in medical journals, including archiving, advertising, media interactions, clinical trial registration, data sharing, and detailed manuscript section-by-section guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent preservation of journal content
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent preservation of journal articles on a journal’s website, or in an independent archive or a credible repository, is essential for the historical record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing an article in its entirety is almost never justified because copies may have been downloaded; archives should be freely accessible or accessible to archive members; deposition in multiple archives is encouraged. If an article is removed for legal reasons, the URL must contain a detailed reason and the article must be retained in the journal’s internal archive. The publisher is responsible for permanent preservation of the journal’s total content and must ensure transfer to a responsible third party on termination. Journal websites should post the date that nonarticle web pages were last updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policy and editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should not be dominated by advertisements, and advertising must not be allowed to influence editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should have formal, explicit, written policies for advertising in print and electronic versions. Best practice prohibits selling ads intended to be juxtaposed with editorial content on the same product. Advertisements should be clearly identifiable. Editors should have full and final authority for approving print and online advertisements and for enforcing advertising policy. Journals should not carry advertisements for products proven to be seriously harmful to health. Editors should ensure enforcement of existing regulatory or industry standards for advertisements or develop their own. The interests of organizations should not control classified or nondisplay advertising (except where required by law). Editors should consider publishing criticisms of advertisements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media interactions and embargo policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors’ interactions with media should balance the public’s right to important information with the risk of premature or inaccurate reporting before peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may use embargo systems to create a level playing field for reporters and to minimize premature reporting; embargo systems operate on honor and lack formal enforcement. Editors can seek agreements with authors not to publicize while under consideration and with media not to release stories before publication in return for cooperation (press releases, advance copies). Exceptional public-health circumstances may justify earlier release, but editors should consult appropriate public health authorities and may waive prepublication publicity policies when necessary. Policies limiting prepublication publicity do not apply to meeting presentations or meeting abstracts. When an article is near publication, editors or staff should assist media (news releases, answering questions, supplying advance copies) contingent on media cooperation with timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective clinical trial registration requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ICMJE recommends that all medical journal editors require registration of clinical trials in a public trials registry at or before the time of first patient consent as a condition of consideration for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE uses the date registration materials were first submitted to a registry as the date of registration; editors may inquire when there is a delay to posting. Approval from an ethics board does not substitute for prospective registration. The purpose is to prevent selective publication/reporting, unnecessary duplication, and to inform patients and ethics boards. Retrospective registration (e.g., at submission) meets none of these purposes and risks inadmissibility; exceptions should be rare, require registration and explanations in the publication, and editors should publish why the exception was allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a clinical trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A clinical trial is any research project that prospectively assigns people or groups to an intervention, with or without concurrent comparison or control groups, to study the relationship between a health-related intervention and a health outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Health-related interventions include drugs, surgical procedures, devices, behavioral treatments, educational programs, dietary interventions, quality improvement interventions, and process-of-care changes. Health outcomes include any biomedical or health-related measures, including pharmacokinetic measures and adverse events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable registries and minimum dataset
rubrics_metrics.description: ICMJE accepts registration in any WHO ICTRP primary register that includes the minimum acceptable 24-item trial registration data set or in ClinicalTrials.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable registries are publicly accessible at no charge, open to all prospective registrants, managed by a not-for-profit, have mechanisms to ensure validity of registration data, and are electronically searchable. Registrations must include the minimum 24-item WHO data set at time of registration and before enrollment. Authors who register in non–WHO-approved registries should also register in a WHO-approved registry. Trials of devices must opt out of lock boxes at ClinicalTrials.gov to meet policy. The ICMJE considers inadequate registrations to include missing any of the 24 fields, uninformative field entries, or non–publicly accessible registrations (e.g., lock-boxed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary analyses and registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary data analyses of primary clinical trials should not be registered as separate clinical trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary analyses should reference the original trial registration number of the primary trial. Authors should ensure compliance with funding and regulatory requirements for aggregate results reporting in registries. Editors will not consider posting of limited trial results in registries (brief structured abstracts or tables) as prior publication for the purposes of journal publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and citation of trial registration numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should publish the trial registration number at the end of the abstract and authors should list the registration number when first using a trial acronym.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data are deposited in a public repository or used in a secondary analysis, authors should state repository name and unique persistent data-set identifier at the end of the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors’ access to supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: All authors should have the ability to review the data supporting study results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In collaborations between academic and nonacademic institutions, at least one author from the academic institution should have accessed primary data and participate in analysis. In sponsored research, authors' access should be expressly provided in agreements. Editors may ask which specific authors had access and participated in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing statement requirements for clinical trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts submitted to ICMJE journals that report clinical trials must contain a data sharing statement; trials beginning enrollment on/after 1 January 2019 must include a data sharing plan in registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data sharing statements must indicate whether individual deidentified participant data (including data dictionaries) will be shared ("undecided" is not acceptable); what data will be shared; whether related documents (protocol, SAP) will be available; when data will become available and for how long; and the access criteria (with whom, for what analyses, and mechanism). If the plan changes after registration it should be updated in the statement and the registry. Table 1 provides illustrative examples of acceptable statements (range of sharing options, timelines, access mechanisms, and review committees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities and credit for shared data
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of secondary analyses using shared data must attest compliance with original terms, reference the data’s unique persistent identifier, explain how their analyses differ, and recognize the efforts of data generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary analysts should reference the unique persistent identifier to provide credit and allow searching. Those using data collected by others should seek collaboration with the original investigators where possible. Data generators deserve substantial credit; when collaboration is not possible, their efforts must still be recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMRAD structure and manuscript formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Original research articles are usually divided into Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion (IMRAD); other article types may require different formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IMRAD reflects the process of scientific discovery. Articles often need subheadings within sections. Electronic formats allow supplementary materials, layering, cross-linking, and extraction; supplementary electronic-only material should be submitted and peer-reviewed simultaneously with the primary manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are encouraged (and some journals require) to follow reporting guidelines appropriate to study design (e.g., CONSORT, STROBE, PRISMA, STARD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting guidelines help authors describe studies sufficiently for evaluation. Authors should consult SAGER for sex and gender reporting. Review manuscripts should describe methods for locating, selecting, extracting, and synthesizing data (mandatory for systematic reviews). Good sources include the EQUATOR Network and NLM’s reporting guidelines resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The title page usually includes article title, author information, disclaimers, sources of support, word count, and sometimes numbers of tables and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article title should be a distilled description and, where appropriate, include study design to aid retrieval. Some journals require a short title (often ≤40 characters) and submission systems may restrict title length. Author information should list highest degrees (if published), department(s), institutions, and full contact details; list corresponding author telephone and email. The ICMJE encourages listing ORCID identifiers. Disclaimers might state that views are authors’ own. Sources of support should include only direct supports that facilitated the work. Word counts should exclude abstract, acknowledgments, tables, figure legends, and references; separate abstract word count is useful. Specify number of figures and tables to allow editorial staff to confirm completeness and assess fit to space limits. Disclosure of relationships/activities for each author must be part of the manuscript; ICMJE provides a uniform Disclosure Form journals are encouraged to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract content and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Original research, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses require structured abstracts that provide context, purpose, basic procedures, main findings (with effect sizes and statistical/clinical significance if possible), principal conclusions, and limitations without overinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical trial abstracts should include CONSORT-identified essential items. Funding sources should be listed separately after the abstract and include only direct support of the work. Because abstracts are often the only indexed portion, authors must ensure accuracy and consistency with the full text; editors/authors should check consistency during revision. Abstract formats differ by journal and must follow the chosen journal’s required format. The ICMJE recommends including the trial registration number at the end of the abstract and repository identifiers when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction section expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context/background for the study, state the specific purpose or research objective/hypothesis, cite only directly pertinent references, and do not include data or conclusions from the work being reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction should succinctly set up the research question or hypothesis without presenting results or conclusions from the current study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods section: clarity and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Methods section should make clear how and why a study was done and be sufficiently detailed so others with access to data could reproduce the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only information available at the time the study plan/protocol was written; information obtained during the study belongs in Results. Describe the role of organizations contracted to help conduct research. Include a statement of approval by an independent review body (ethics committee/IRB). If there is doubt about adherence to the Helsinki Declaration, explain rationale and show explicit approval of doubtful aspects. Describe AI technology use in sufficient detail to enable replication (tool used, version, prompts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and description of participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly describe selection of observational or experimental participants, including eligibility and exclusion criteria and a description of the source population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for inclusion of representative populations and at minimum provide descriptive data for variables such as age, sex, and ethnicity. Comment on representativeness of the study sample relative to the larger population of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex, gender, race, and ethnicity reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure correct use of the terms sex (biological) and gender (identity), report sex and/or gender of participants unless inappropriate, define how race/ethnicity were determined and justify relevance, and use neutral, precise, respectful language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the study involves an exclusive population (e.g., single sex), justify why. If race/ethnicity was not collected, explain why. Treat race and ethnicity as social, not biological constructs and interpret results accordingly. Avoid terminology that might stigmatize participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection and measurement reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify main and secondary objectives (primary and secondary outcomes); identify methods, equipment (with manufacturer), and procedures in sufficient detail to allow reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give references to established methods and brief descriptions for less-known methods; describe new or substantially modified methods with reasons for use and limitations. Identify drugs and chemicals precisely (generic names, doses, routes). Identify appropriate scientific/gene names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe statistical methods with enough detail to enable a knowledgeable reader with the data to judge appropriateness and verify results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify findings and present appropriate indicators of error or uncertainty (confidence intervals). Avoid relying solely on P values. Reference standard works for design and statistics (with pages). Define statistical terms, abbreviations, and symbols. Specify statistical software and versions. Distinguish prespecified from exploratory analyses, including subgroup analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results presentation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Present results in logical sequence with main findings first; do not repeat all table/figure data in text; provide data on all primary and secondary outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place extra or technical details in appendices or electronic supplements. Report numeric results as absolute numbers in addition to derivatives (percentages). Restrict tables/figures to those needed to explain arguments and assess data. Use graphs instead of tables when appropriate and avoid duplication between graphs and tables. Avoid nontechnical uses of statistical terms (e.g., 'random', 'normal', 'significant'). Routinely separate reporting by demographic variables (age, sex) unless compelling reasons not to, which should be explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion content and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin discussion by briefly summarizing main findings, explore mechanisms and explanations, emphasize new/important aspects, state limitations, and explore implications for research and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss influence of variables (e.g., sex/gender) where appropriate. Do not repeat detailed data. Link conclusions to study goals but avoid unqualified or unsupported statements. Distinguish clinical from statistical significance. Avoid economic claims without appropriate data/analyses. Avoid claiming priority or referencing incomplete work. State new hypotheses clearly as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: sourcing and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide direct references to original research whenever possible; cite published articles rather than abstracts; avoid referencing predatory journals; label preprints clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using references to promote self-interest. When citing personal communications, only do so if essential and with written permission; cite as '(personal communication, name, date)'. Authors are responsible for accurate citations and should verify references using bibliographic sources or original sources. Ensure no references cite retracted articles except in context of the retraction; use PubMed as authoritative for retractions. Number references consecutively in the order first mentioned. Follow NLM sample references/Citing Medicine for style; consult specific journal requirements for electronic references formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables: preparation and citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare tables according to specific journal requirements; number tables consecutively and supply short, self-explanatory titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tables can be imported into the journal’s publication software to avoid errors. Titles should let readers understand the table without returning to the text. Be sure each table is cited in the text.
